\chapter{Si --- If, and the Word Yes Is Made Of}
\label{ch:si}
\hlchaptermodality{196}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can make a real condition with si and the present.}

I can make a real condition with si and the present.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[si]{si}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-si}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Sí}.) Now the pair from the accent chapter: \emph{el} and \emph{él}. Same letters, one accent, two words.

Today you meet the third member of that family — and it is \emph{sí} with the accent taken off.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{si}} — if
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{sī} meant \emph{if}. Spanish kept it unchanged.

And the \emph{sí} you already know — \textbf{yes} — is that same word with a \textbf{pointing particle} stuck on the end: Latin \textbf{sīc} is \emph{sī} + \emph{-ce}, roughly \emph{if-so}, which came to mean \emph{thus}, \emph{that way}, and finally \textbf{yes}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{si} $\leftarrow$ \emph{sī} — \textbf{if}  ·  \emph{sí} $\leftarrow$ \emph{sī} + \emph{-ce} — \textbf{thus} $\to$ \textbf{yes}
\end{quote}

So \emph{yes} is literally \emph{if}, pointed at. The accent is the only thing keeping them apart on the page, and it is doing the same job it did for \emph{el} and \emph{él}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the real condition}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{For something that really might happen: \emph{si} + present, then present.}
\end{quote}

No new verb form. You already have every piece:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Si tengo tiempo, hablo español.} & If I have time, I speak Spanish. \\
\emph{Si llueve, no voy.} & If it rains, I don't go. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both halves sit in the present, and the sentence is about something genuinely possible — today, tomorrow, whenever.

The order can flip, and the comma simply goes away:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Hablo español si tengo tiempo.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Si tengo tiempo, hablo español}
  \item \emph{Si llueve, no voy}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which tense goes on each side of a real condition? (\textbf{Present}, both.)

And what separates \emph{if} from \emph{yes}? (One \textbf{accent} — and a pointing particle, two thousand years ago.)
\end{tcolorbox}
